subject: Banking
title: Collateral and Secured Lending
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Collateral and Secured Lending.

hook.text: A mortgage is cheap because the bank can take your house.

buildup.text: Collateral reduces lender risk. If you default, the bank sells the asset to recover its money.

discovery.text: Homes, cars, and savings accounts can all serve as collateral. The better the collateral, the lower the interest rate.

twist.text: In a crash, the asset securing the loan can sink below the debt and expose both sides.

climax.text: Collateral makes lending safer until the collateral's value drops.

punchline.text: Your house secures the mortgage. If home values drop, the safety disappears.

quiz.question: Why do mortgages have lower interest rates than personal loans?
options: The home serves as collateral the bank can seize

details.summary: Secured lending requires borrowers to pledge assets like property, vehicles, or savings as collateral that the lender can seize if the loan is not repaid. Collateral reduces lender risk and typically results in lower interest rates for borrowers.
details.whyItMatters: Collateral is the oldest risk management tool in lending. It determines who can access affordable credit and who faces higher rates. Understanding collateral explains the vast gap between mortgage rates and credit card rates.
takeaways: Collateral gives lenders recourse to seize assets if borrowers default
Secured loans carry significantly lower interest rates than unsecured loans
Home equity is the most common collateral for individual borrowers

faq.question: Why are mortgage rates so much lower than credit card rates?
faq.answer: A mortgage is secured by your home, giving the lender a valuable asset to recover losses if you default. Credit cards are unsecured, meaning the lender has nothing to seize. The higher risk of unsecured lending is reflected in higher rates.

faq.question: What happens if the collateral value drops below the loan amount?
faq.answer: This creates a situation called being underwater. The lender's security is impaired because selling the collateral would not fully recover the loan. This was widespread during the 2008 housing crisis when home values plummeted below mortgage balances.
